title: Official talk
job: Announcements, offices and counters: the formal register you hear
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: How Russian says a thing with NO DOER — three devices, and a sign or an announcement is built from one of them. (a) The SHORT-FORM PARTICIPLE as the whole predicate: zakrýto, otkrýto, zányato, zapreshchenó, with no verb beside it. (b) The REFLEXIVE PASSIVE, which is L3-M1's -sya doing a third job: magazín zakryváyetsya, the shop closes, with nothing said about who closes it. (c) The BARE THIRD-PERSON PLURAL: Vam pozvonyát, Zdes' ne kúryat — a plural verb, no subject at all, meaning one, they, or somebody.

English reaches for the passive — you will be called, smoking is not permitted — and Russian's commonest answer contains no passive whatever: a bare plural verb with the subject slot empty. Vam pozvonyát is literally they-will-ring to-you, and nobody is meant by they. Supplying oní puts real people in the sentence and changes what it says; building a byt' passive gives something a station would never print.

The short participles are a WORD LIST, not a system: learn zakrýto, otkrýto, zányato and zapreshchenó as four labels, because the machine that makes them is L5's. AND EACH ONE'S STRESS IS ITS OWN: zakrýto and zányato are front-heavy, zapreshchenó throws the stress right to the end. There is no pattern to lean on here, so learn each with its acute attached.

The sign words are short, frozen and read like labels, so they cost almost nothing and pay at once: vkhod is the way in, výkhod the way out, zakrýto shut, otkrýto open. None of them takes a verb — a Russian label is a noun or a participle standing alone, and adding yest' to it is what marks a foreigner.

The register of an announcement is vy from end to end and has two fixed openers. uvazháyemye passazhíry, respected passengers, is how a platform or a carriage addresses everybody; prósim vas plus an infinitive, we ask you to, is how it makes a request. Neither has an informal twin: there is no ty version of a public announcement, so nothing new about politeness is opened here.

words.note: The label on a locked door. Neuter with nothing to agree with; zakrýt for a masculine thing, zakrýta for a feminine one. Stress on the ý, never on the last syllable.
The other half of the same sign, built the same way. It is a state, not an act: L4-M1's otkróyte is the command to open something.

sentences.trap: There is no is in either half, and none is missing. English needs it's closed; Russian's sign is the participle on its own, and putting a verb beside it is what makes a learner's Russian sound translated.
sentences.sound: za-KRY-ta — the ý is the hard Russian y, made with the tongue pulled back, and the final o reduces to a.

variations.cue: The shop is shut, but the chemist is open.
variations.changed: real nouns in the sentence, so the participles agree with them
a neuter noun, which happens to want the same form as the bare sign

mistake.why: zakrýt is the masculine form and wants a masculine thing to agree with. A sign naming nothing takes the neuter, which is why every door in Russia says zakrýto and not zakrýt.

sentences.usage: Reading a card in a window, or telling someone what it said.
sentences.mnemonic: A Russian sign is one word and no verb: zakrýto, otkrýto, and the door has spoken.

words.note: The printed prohibition, and the one short participle here with END stress — zapreshchenó, not zapréshcheno. It takes a plain infinitive after it.

sentences.trap: English turns the verb into a noun — smoking is prohibited. Russian leaves it an infinitive: zapreshchenó kurít', prohibited to-smoke. There is no Russian noun to build here and no -ing to look for.
sentences.sound: za-pri-shchi-NO — four syllables with the stress dead last, and shch is one long soft sh.

variations.changed: a different infinitive in the same slot
the bare sign, with the infinitive in front

mistake.why: ne mózhno is not Russian at all. Spoken, the word is L3-M4's nel'zyá; printed on a wall, it is zapreshchenó. Neither is built by negating mózhno.

sentences.usage: Reading a wall, a platform, or the back of a door.
sentences.mnemonic: The longest of the four labels earns the stress at the very end: za-pri-shchi-NO.

sentences.cue: You'll get a call tomorrow morning.

words.note: A plural verb with the subject slot deliberately empty — the ordinary way to say you will be called. Nobody is meant by they, and naming one changes the sentence.

sentences.trap: This is where an English speaker builds a passive and gets nothing usable. Russian does not say you will be called; it says they-will-ring-you and leaves they unfilled.
sentences.sound: paz-va-NYAT — stress on the last syllable, and the ya there is a full open a after a soft n.

variations.changed: where the call comes from, still with no person named

variations.cue: You'll get a call in the evening.
variations.changed: a different time on the same empty-subject frame

mistake.why: The passive an English speaker reaches for, assembled out of L1-M5's búdete and a participle that does not exist. Russian's answer to you will be called is the bare plural verb, and there is nothing to build.

sentences.usage: What a clerk tells you as you leave the counter.
sentences.mnemonic: No doer, so no subject — Russian just makes the verb plural and moves on.

sentences.cue: People don't smoke here — it isn't allowed.

words.note: The same empty-subject plural as pozvonyát, used of a custom rather than an event. Front-stressed: KU-ryat, from L3-M4's kurít'.
The third-plural of L1-M4's govorít, and the commonest of these subjectless verbs — zdes' govoryát po-rússki, Russian is spoken here.

sentences.trap: Do not put a subject in. Zdes' oní ne kúryat means those particular people are not smoking; Zdes' ne kúryat means it is not done here, which is what a Russian actually says.
sentences.sound: KU-ryat — front-stressed, and the final -yat is short and soft, quite unlike pozvonyát's ending.

variations.changed: a different verb on the same subjectless frame
the bare rule, with the explanation dropped

mistake.why: Correct Russian about a specific group of people you can point at. As a house rule it is wrong: the whole force of the device is that the subject slot stays empty.

sentences.usage: Explaining a rule that nobody in particular made.
sentences.mnemonic: Leave the subject out and the rule applies to everyone; put one in and it applies to them.

sentences.cue: The train departs at seven o'clock.

words.note: L3-M1's -sya in a third job: not washing oneself, but a passive with nobody doing it. The train is dispatched, and the -sya is what removes the dispatcher.
The noun on the departures board. A separate word from the verb, not one of its forms, so it is learnt separately — as is pribýtiye, arrival.

sentences.trap: English says the train departs and the train is dispatched with two different verbs. Russian has one verb plus -sya, and it covers both without saying who did the dispatching.
sentences.sound: at-prav-LYA-yit-sa — five syllables, stress in the middle, and the final -tsya is said ts-a.

variations.changed: the board's version — a noun, and no verb at all
a different hour, with chasóv left off as speech does

mistake.why: Without -sya the verb needs something to dispatch, and the sentence goes looking for an object it never finds. The -sya is not decoration here; it is what makes the train the thing that leaves.

sentences.usage: Repeating what the board or the tannoy just said.
sentences.mnemonic: Add -sya and the doer disappears: the train dispatches itself.

words.note: The event, where zakrýto is the state. The shop shuts at eight and is shut afterwards, and Russian marks the difference with a verb against a participle.

sentences.trap: English uses closes for both the act and the sign. Russian does not: zakryváyetsya happens at eight, zakrýto is true from eight onwards, and a shop is never described with the wrong one.
sentences.sound: za-kry-VA-yit-sa — the stress sits on the va, two syllables further along than in zakrýto.

variations.changed: an hour earlier
an adverb instead of a clock time

mistake.why: Without -sya the shop is closing something else, and the listener waits for the object. The reflexive ending is the whole device: it lets the shop be the thing that shuts.

sentences.usage: Answering do you know when they shut?
sentences.mnemonic: zakryváyetsya is the clock striking; zakrýto is what the door says afterwards.

sentences.display: Uvazháyemye passazhíry, póyezd pribyváyet chérez chas.
sentences.script: Уважаемые пассажиры, поезд прибывает через час.
sentences.cue: Attention passengers, the train arrives in an hour.
sentences.literal: Respected passengers, train arrives through hour.

words.note: The opener of every public address in Russian, and untranslatable word for word — it does the work English gives to ladies and gentlemen or to a bare attention.
Passengers. Costs nothing to recognise, and the double s is written but said single. Stress on the zhí.
The arrivals half of the board, opposite otpravlyáyetsya. No -sya on this one: a train arrives by itself and needs nothing removed.

sentences.trap: uvazháyemye is not a greeting and cannot start a conversation with one person. It addresses a crowd, and out of a loudspeaker it is neutral rather than grand.
sentences.sound: u-va-ZHA-ye-mye pa-sa-ZHY-ry — two long words, each stressed on its third syllable.

variations.cue: Attention passengers, the train is arriving.
variations.changed: the announcement with no time in it

variations.cue: The train arrives in an hour.
variations.changed: the fact on its own, without the address

mistake.display: Dorogíye passazhíry, póyezd pribyváyet chérez chas.
mistake.script: Дорогие пассажиры, поезд прибывает через час.
mistake.why: dorogíye is dear, which is how a letter to friends begins. A station, an office and a bank all say uvazháyemye, and the difference is heard immediately.

sentences.usage: Understanding a platform announcement — this is a listening sentence, not a speaking one.
sentences.mnemonic: Every Russian tannoy opens with respect: uvazháyemye first, news second.

sentences.display: Vnimániye, vkhod zdes', a výkhod tam.
sentences.script: Внимание, вход здесь, а выход там.
sentences.cue: Attention: the way in is here, the way out is over there.
sentences.literal: Attention, entrance here, and exit there.

words.note: The one word that opens an announcement when there is no crowd to name. Printed with an exclamation mark, spoken as a flat warning.
The label over a door you may go through. One syllable, and the v is voiced straight into the kh.
Its opposite, and the pair differ only in the first syllable: vkhod in, výkhod out. This one is front-stressed and has two syllables.

sentences.trap: Neither label takes a verb. Vkhod zdes' is the whole sentence, and adding yest' turns a sign into a claim that entrances exist.
sentences.sound: VY-khat — the ý is that hard back y again, and the final d hardens to a t.

variations.changed: the shortest form the sign takes

variations.cue: The exit is to the left, the entrance to the right.
variations.changed: L2-M4's directions doing the pointing instead of here and there

mistake.why: L1-M7's yest' says there exists, which no sign has ever needed. A label is a noun and a place, and the verb between them is exactly what Russian leaves out.

sentences.usage: Reading your way through a station, a museum or a car park.
sentences.mnemonic: vkhod in, výkhod out — one letter apart, and the y is the one going out.

words.note: A seat on a train, a place in a queue, a spot on a shelf. Neuter, which is why the participle beside it is zányato.
Front-stressed — ZA-nya-ta — unlike zapreshchenó. L3-M5 taught this word of a busy PERSON; the neuter form here is the one a seat, a table or a line takes.

sentences.trap: The stress is the whole difficulty. zányato and zapreshchenó are the same kind of word with opposite stress, and neither can be guessed from the other.
sentences.sound: ZA-nya-ta — heavy first syllable, then two light ones falling away.

variations.changed: without the apology in front
no noun at all, which is how it is usually said

mistake.why: That is the masculine form, and it belongs to L3-M5's busy person. mésto is neuter, so a taken seat is zányato — the ending is the only thing telling a listener which you mean.

sentences.usage: Keeping a seat for someone, politely and without a fight.
sentences.mnemonic: A person is busy and a seat is taken with one Russian word — only the ending tells a listener which you mean.

sentences.display: Prósim vas ne kurít' na stántsii.
sentences.script: Просим вас не курить на станции.
sentences.cue: We ask you not to smoke at the station.
sentences.literal: We-ask you not to-smoke at station.

words.note: The polite half of an announcement: prósim vas plus an infinitive. The we is the institution, never a group of people you could count.

sentences.trap: prósim vas is softer than it looks in English, where we ask you to sounds like a warning. In Russian it is the ordinary printed request and carries no threat at all.
sentences.sound: PRO-sim vas — front-stressed, the o full and round because it is stressed.

variations.cue: We ask you not to smoke.
variations.changed: the request with no place attached

variations.cue: We ask you to pass on the message.
variations.changed: a positive request, with L2-M7's infinitive in the slot

mistake.display: Vy ne dolzhný kurít' na stántsii.
mistake.script: Вы не должны курить на станции.
mistake.why: Correct Russian, and it accuses: L3-M4's dolzhný tells this particular person what they are obliged to do. An announcement addresses nobody, so it asks — prósim vas.

sentences.usage: The sentence a loudspeaker says just before someone lights up.
sentences.mnemonic: The institution says we and asks; it never says you must.
